facts.headline: Every Thursday, mothers still march this square in silence
facts.body_html: Since 1977, the Madres de Plaza de Mayo have circled this square in white headscarves, carrying photos of children who disappeared under military rule. The protest began when public gatherings were banned — and it still happens every Thursday.

facts.headline: A 19-year-old was buried here — and woke up inside her coffin
facts.body_html: Rufina Cambaceres collapsed and was declared dead in 1902, then buried at Recoleta Cemetery. The next night, staff found her coffin moved and her fingers bloodied from clawing at the lid — she had likely suffered a cataleptic fit and woken up entombed.

facts.headline: A tango singer painted this street with leftover boat paint
facts.body_html: Caminito was a disused rail siding until tango singer Benito Quinquela Martín painted it into Argentina's most photographed street. The clashing colors trace back to immigrant dockworkers who painted their houses with whatever ship paint was left over.

facts.headline: A skyscraper built as a 3D map of Dante's Hell, Purgatory and Heaven
facts.body_html: Palacio Barolo's 22 floors map directly onto the Divine Comedy — hell in the basement, heaven at the top — and its height in meters matches Dante's 100 cantos exactly. Its rooftop spire was even built to align with the Southern Cross.

facts.headline: The president's pink palace may owe its color to cow's blood
facts.body_html: Casa Rosada's signature pink is rumored to come from a 19th-century trick: mixing cow's blood into whitewash to fight off humidity damage. The balcony where Eva Perón famously addressed crowds still overlooks the square today.

facts.headline: This stadium's nickname came from a birthday present
facts.body_html: Boca Juniors' stadium gets its nickname, La Bombonera ('the chocolate box'), from a box of chocolates the architect kept carrying to design meetings — its shape looked just like the tight, steep-walled stadium the team was building.

facts.headline: Tango was too scandalous for Argentina — until Paris said it was fine
facts.body_html: Tango was born in the cramped immigrant tenements of San Telmo in the late 1800s, and Argentina's upper class banned it as indecent. It only became respectable at home after it turned fashionable in Paris first.
